summary: For ages 10–11, interpret and construct pie charts. The full 360° circle is one data set; each sector angle is the category fraction of the total multiplied by 360°. Recover a count by multiplying the sector fraction by the known total. Compute the angles, draw them with a protractor, label categories, and verify each against the table as well as checking their sum. This topic does not assess line-graph mastery, which belongs to the separate Line graphs topic (mt_HlNSurPVDp).
misconceptions: Reading a pie sector as a raw quantity rather than a proportion of the whole — or trying to read an actual count off the chart without using the total
Calculating a sector angle by dividing 360° by the frequency (instead of taking the frequency as a fraction of the total, of 360°)
Calculating a sector angle by multiplying the frequency by the total frequency
Not checking that the sector angles sum to 360°

activities.title: Live pie-chart builder from class data
steps: Enter a class data table into a tool that repartitions a circle in real time, e.g. favourite pet: dog 12, cat 6, rabbit 6, with 24 children in all
Watch dog's 12-out-of-24 sector swing open to fill exactly half the circle, with a label ticking over to 180° and 50%
Compute each sector angle yourself as (frequency ÷ total) × 360°: dog 12/24 × 360° = 180°, cat and rabbit 6/24 × 360° = 90° each
Add the sector angles and confirm they sum to 360° before drawing

Deliberately try the tempting wrong method 360 ÷ 12 = 30° for dog (and 360 ÷ 6 = 60° for the others) and watch the sectors fall well short of closing, totalling only 150° and leaving 210° of the circle empty
Use a protractor-construction mode to lay off each computed angle from a starting radius
Use a 'show actual numbers' toggle that stays greyed out until the total is entered, making visible that a sector is a proportion, not a count
activities.insight: A pie sector's angle is the category's share of the whole circle — (frequency ÷ total) × 360° — not 360 divided by the frequency and not frequency times the total; and the sectors must sum to one whole turn, 360°.

activities.title: Recover a count from a sector and the total
steps: Read a given pie chart where a sector's angle is stated, e.g. 'the walk sector is a right angle, 90°, and 40 children travel in all — how many walk?'
Work out the sector's fraction of the whole: 90° is a quarter of 360°, so a quarter of 40 = 10 children walk
Try a second: 'a sector is 72° and there are 20 children altogether — how many is that?' (72/360 × 20 = 4)
State explicitly which number came from the chart (the angle/fraction) and which from the given total (the count)
activities.insight: To get an actual quantity from a pie chart you must combine the sector's fraction with the known total; the raw count is not visible on the chart itself.

activities.title: Compare same-size sectors from different totals
steps: Compare two pie charts: a class of 30 and a class of 12 that both have a 'football' sector of the same size (say 120°, a third of the circle)
Decide whether the equal-size slices mean the same number of children, and justify
Work out the two actual counts using each chart's own total: a third of 30 = 10 versus a third of 12 = 4, noticing that equal fractions give different counts
activities.insight: A sector is a proportion of ITS OWN total; equal-looking sectors from different totals can represent different counts.

activities.title: Scorable checks on interpret and partial-construct skills
steps: Complete a fill-in task: 'the bus sector is 120°, there are 36 children, so ___ take the bus' (12)
Compute a sector angle from a table in a single step and enter it
Answer a multiple-choice item that includes the '360 ÷ frequency' answer as a tempting wrong option, and explain why it is wrong
activities.insight: Reading a sector with the total and computing a sector angle can be checked for accuracy; recognising a correct angle is not the same as constructing a whole chart.

activities.title: Annotated reference charts for reviewing structure
steps: On a labelled pie chart, reveal each sector's angle, fraction/percentage and — given the total — its count, to confirm how the three relate
Use these as worked examples when checking your own constructions or interpretations
activities.insight: Relating the angle, fraction and count on an annotated pie chart can support review, but independent construction must be checked separately.

checkQuestion: First interpret: a pie chart represents 60 children and its walk sector is 90°. How many children walk? Then construct: a table has apple 10, banana 5 and orange 5, total 20. Calculate every sector angle, draw the pie chart with a protractor, label the categories, and explain how you checked it.
checkAnswer: The walk sector is 90/360 = 1/4 (25%) of the whole, so 1/4 × 60 = 15 children walk. For the fruit chart: apple 10/20 = 1/2 (50%), so 10/20 × 360° = 180°; banana and orange are each 5/20 = 1/4 (25%), so 5/20 × 360° = 90° each. The angles total 360° and each sector agrees with its table fraction. A completed labelled drawing is required for construction; computing or selecting an angle alone does not demonstrate the full skill.
